Mr. Speaker, rather than include in my congratulations only the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I want to include most of those who have thus far taken part in this traditional debate, because my personal feeling is that unusual enthusiasm has been brought to bear during the discussion up to the present moment. It might be, of course, that because of the fact that, as is generally agreed, we are in the last session before the election, more effort and more vigour is being employed with regard to the discussions at hand. The vehemence on the part of the supporters of

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale the government seems to lie in the typical direction of whitewashing the government program; and from the standpoint of those of us who are in the opposition, we are more vigorous in our criticisms of government policy. I suppose that is as it should be, or at least that it is inevitable under our party system.
It is, however, almost too much to expect members of the opposition to agree that the government record is without spot and without blemish entirely, as some of those who have spoken in support of the government would tend to suggest. In fact there are so many skeletons out of the cupboard at the present time that it is going to be extremely difficult indeed to bury them. This fact has become increasingly obvious as we have had recent expressions of public opinion from across Canada.
I was impressed by a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) during his remarks the other day. Since coming into the chamber I have found that the Prime Minister endeavours to be fair in most of his remarks, except perhaps sometimes when he finds himself in bad company; and that is inevitable under the circumstances. The observation he made with regard to the role of the official opposition in the chamber impressed me. As recorded at page 34 of Hansard, he said:
... I extend congratulations to the Leader of the Opposition for the very frank, and perhaps some of us may sometimes think severe, criticism of the actions of the government. It is a part of our democratic institutions that there should be someone recognized in our official organizations whose duty it is to watch and criticize what is being done by the advisers of the crown, and I think it is helpful that that should be so.
That is a fair and unbiased appraisal of the role of the opposition. Regardless of the discussion which took place the other day as to ghost writers, I am sure he was speaking from personal experience so far as that matter is concerned. While on the subject of ghost writers-and I notice that it was raised again this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton)- may I say that I think the final word arises from an incident that occurred some time ago in the United States when a politician who had grown accustomed to the habit of relying on the efforts of ghost writers on one occasion found himself placed in an extremely embarrassing position. He had neglected to read the speech before he began to give it. He progressed through pages 1, 2 and 3. Everything was going well until he got to page 4, which he found blank with the exception of one fine at the top. That line said: "You


are on your own, you old windbag; I quit." That is the last comment that should be made in regard to ghost-writing in this chamber.
In contrast to the Prime Minister's reference to the role of the opposition, I find sometimes that more eager and rash members of the government group have a different opinion. It has been expressed, mostly outside this chamber, to the effect that "an opposition member can be of little or no service to the people and can only be, like the leader of the official opposition, an obstructionist and a destructive critic". I am glad to see that the Prime Minister does not agree with that viewpoint. Actually, from what I have already observed in the chamber, I am glad that we do have an opposition group to keep a close check on government activities. I am sure the claim that has been made three times already during this debate by various members is true, namely that whatever can be said concerning the government, it cannot be accused of reckless dishonesty, graft and other similar activities such as sometimes occur south of the border. To back up that observation the Ottawa Journal has been referred to.
Apparently that paper is a journal of considerable reputation, if one is to judge from the emphasis and the confidence placed in it by government speakers. It is significant that that journal on various occasions has declared that the present opposition leadership in this house is the best that Canada has seen since confederation. I am sure if we rely upon the opinion of that paper in one instance, we must accept it as an unbiased opinion in the other.
The members of the government should be very grateful to the opposition in this regard. The reason things are more closely under control in our House of Commons, under our parliamentary system, is that the ministers are directly responsible to the elected representatives, and not as in the United States more or less operating outside of the framework of the elected bodies. In that country the ministers have to report to the electorate only at four-year intervals.
Furthermore, the impact of the opposition criticism can be seen in some of the legislation that is brought in. For example, in the speech from the throne reference was made to fair employment practices; to changes in attitude regarding television; to the abolition of the radio licence, and a rather more solicitous approach to the handling of commonwealth relations problems, all of which have been advocated by members

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale
of the official opposition for some considerable time. We can come to the conclusion, however, that there are still some things that have been left undone, judging from the remarks on this side in reference to taxation, inflation, extravagance, failure to ease means test restrictions on war veterans' allowances and also on pensions for the blind. These are subjects which have come up on several occasions already in this house in this debate on the speech from the throne. I am not going to deal with these matters because they are of general concern to all Canadians, and they have already been dealt with at some considerable length by other speakers. I shall rather, as did the speaker who preceded me in this debate, concentrate on problems that might be regarded as peculiar to the west.
I find myself in sympathy with a good many of the viewpoints expressed by the previous speaker. Because the voice of the west in this House of Commons is rather a weak one from the standpoint of numerical representation, I think that we might well concentrate on our particular difficulties. Not only is it a weak voice; it is growing weaker as a result of what has been referred to by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) as the fairest redistribution ever undertaken in the Dominion of Canada. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I am afraid that depends on your own viewpoint. I am sure that my colleague the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and myself do not agree that it is the fairest redistribution that has been carried out in the history of Canada. As I say, it depends on your own viewpoint.
I do feel, along with the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore), that there is some misunderstanding concerning our problems in the west, and this misunderstanding goes further than the realm of football. The west, along with Canada generally, has been feeling the effects of the industrial revolution, only our boom might be described as a quiet one, rather than one of the gigantic proportions that we see here in central Canada. The main reason for the relative slowness of development of the prairies of course arises from the effects of centralization. Centralization of population has been mentioned tonight, industrial development, and also more recently, since we became faced with the threat of aggression, the distribution of defence contracts. It is fairly generally understood that the bulk of the contracts are finding their way to the industries of the central provinces rather than to the industrial potential on the prairies. I surveyed the situation in my own constitu-68108-Hi
ency before I left, and found that there was very little change so far as defence contracts are concerned.
Then too, of course, we were a long time recovering from the effects of the depression. In the province of Manitoba we have had a government which has established quite a record for longevity. In fact it has broken the record established by this government by a considerable number of years. We have had a government in office continuously since 1922, and it has not been overly enthusiastic in promoting provincial welfare. In fact we might even go so far as to say it has been extremely cautious, but there is a gradual awakening in this regard, and this awakening comes from the civil service more than it does from direct government policy. The assistant deputy minister of the Manitoba department of industry and commerce, in speaking to a chamber of commerce gathering in Swan River, said that Manitobans must become as industrially minded as they are agriculturally minded if they wish to continue to progress. Or, to express it another way, agriculture must accept its new partners, oil and general industrial development. Actually that partnership is well under way in the province of Manitoba.
That is a statement that should be selfevident, particularly during these post-war years, but it does not seem to be so in certain responsible circles. For example, our Manitoba minister speaking recently in Preece-ville, Saskatchewan, criticized the trend toward industrialization on the prairies, claiming it to be a revival of what he termed Tory protectionism, whatever that may be. I think the charge actually arose from a speech made recently by the Leader of the Opposition in regard to Canada's golden future, suggesting that we might better benefit ourselves by processing our own raw material rather than by allowing ourselves to be despoiled. That hits directly at our problem of industrialization on the prairies.
The reasoning behind the minister's statement was to the effect that such local processing of our natural resources would disturb world trade, cutting off the world markets for our agricultural products. As I look at that statement objectively I think it is merely an attempt to revive the old technique of dividing and conquering through the process of arousing regional prejudices. That worked perhaps at one time during the twenties, when the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec were industrializing very rapidly, when certain protective measures were exercised in their favour, and the old cry of protectionism on the prairies had its effect. But so far as I can see from a study of the economics of the prairies, this is as dead as the

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale dodo bird at the present time because, above all else, the west must industrialize if a balanced economy right across Canada is to be developed. If we are going to increase our population so as to fill these vast and wide open spaces, we must have a diversified economy. In so doing we will not be so dependent upon external markets because we will have developed domestic markets, and we will achieve a level of social and cultural development worthy of a country occupying the strategic importance of Canada in the modern world.
I would say that lack of awareness of new trends on the prairies, particularly in respect to this matter of industrialization, is indicative of a lack of leadership in high government circles. I suppose this is inevitable after long years in office. I was quite amazed- perhaps I should not say "amazed", because it is something more or less universally understood-but I was quite impressed, shall I say, when reading that interesting book "The Incredible Canadian" to find that in 1921 the late Mr. Mackenzie King made the same complaint, that the government had been too long in office, had got out of touch with the people, had become arrogant, and that nothing could be done until public opinion spoke, until the people rose up and protested through their votes.
That is exactly what is happening right across this country at the present time. Incidentally that is why, under our British parliamentary institutions, we have the two-party system, so that as one group grows decrepit with age another has grown vigorous in opposition so that it can take its place and carry on the business of responsible government.
In Manitoba we find evidence of the revival of a vigorous community spirit. The movement is coming from the people in Manitoba and the government is being forced into action in spite of itself. For example, in the city of Brandon we have appointed an industrial commissioner. I believe we are the smallest city to become active in this regard. It has all been done on the local community level, with very little inspiration from higher levels of government.
We have traditions of community activity in this country which are interesting. A few weeks ago it was my experience to go down into that small but unique community of Steinbach and, although it is not in my constituency, I was impressed by what I saw there. Steinbach is the centre of a Mennon-ite community and has been referred to as Manitoba's moneyed mile, because of the weaith and prosperity located there. Right from the beginning the citizens of Steinbach have practised the diversified economy that

the rest of Manitoba is only now beginning to appreciate. They did it in face of the fact that they had no railway communications, and still have none, for that matter. Actually what I found in Steinbach was a way of life, because as you approach the city you see two signs, one of which says "Sign of progress" and, close by, the other saying "Believe on the Lord". I think it is the existence of that sort of spirit among the people-they are God-fearing, thrifty and hard-working-that has made that little community one of the most prosperous, on a proportionate basis, in the whole of Manitoba.
I might add, however, that the same spirit is being felt in other areas of our province. Along with this development, which must inevitably come if we are going to occupy our rightful place in the Canadian economy, we have the general story of oil. My desk-mate and colleague, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Nickle) has told the story of oil in a much more capable way than I could and, because of his background and knowledge, is better able to do so. However, those of us in western Manitoba, particularly in my constituency, have encouraging progress to report. In the Daly oil field west of Virden there are now 14 oil wells capable of producing a thousand barrels a day, so I am informed. It is oil of high quality which will produce gasoline and lubricating oil, as well as crude oil. I understand that oil is being delivered directly to the pipe line operating through the area. So we in Manitoba have the resources, we have the power and we now have the fuel. All we need is a bit of encouragement and inspiration from our senior governments. And perhaps, too, we need a boost in human resources, because no matter what we have in natural resources, nothing can be done until we have a population sufficiently large to carry out the developments to be made there in the near future.
This brings me to the problem of immigration, a subject that has been discussed frequently in recent days across Canada. We have various estimates of the potential Canadian population by the end of the century running all the way from 100 million down to 25 million. Judging from those figures we are due for a very rapid increase in population immediately. One of the chief sources, if not indeed the chief, will be through the process of immigration. In Manitoba we have had it drawn to our attention by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) that he visualizes within the next decade a population of some 100,000 citizens north of 53, where now there are only some 10,000. Certainly there is every encouragement for an increase in population as we view the situation in Manitoba.

Looking at it from the other side of the picture, it would seem that the countries of Europe and the United Kingdom are quite anxious to send their surplus population to our shores. It is estimated, for example, that the United Kingdom alone has a surplus population of approximately 20 million who could be settled in Canada as well as other parts of the commonwealth. I know the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has spoken on this theme on several occasions and is very interested in the problem because he comes from the wide open spaces of the prairies.
Along with the vacillation and the changing moods in regard to prairie industrialization, we also see government vacillation in regard to immigration policy. This was referred to in an article in Saturday Night a few weeks ago, October 4, written by Mr. Michael Barkway, who referred to statements made by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris). It reads in part as follows:
The contradiction between profession and performance has grown wider with each succeeding government statement. Prime Minister St. Laurent has been stumping the country proclaiming that Canada will have a population of 35 million by the end of the century. Walter Harris, the minister directly responsible, is presumably more accurately aware of what the government is actually doing. His prophecy (at London) was a lot more cautious. He forecast 25 million "in the foreseeable future" . . . Deference for his boss, or a misguided attempt to paper over the party's cracks, led to a modified prophecy in a later speech at Montreal. It then became "25 to 35 million people before the end of the century."
The curious contradiction reached a laughable culmination in the official release on immigration in July. July-as Harris had prophesied-showed the first results of the restrictions he introduced earlier in the year. The number of new arrivals was 15 per cent less than July of last year. Their origins were even more drastically changed. The proportion of immigrants from Britain continued the marked increase which started last winter. Last year they were 15 per cent of the total. In the first five months of 1952 they were 23 per cent. In July they were more than 28 per cent.
Now, there seems to be some vacillation in policy, even though it was stated in the minister's speech last July, as I recall, that immigration policy cannot be a stop and go affair. If there is any opposition to immigration it does not come from the prairies, which are urgently in need of population if they are to develop their program of industrialization.
It is interesting to compare this policy with the record of previous immigration ministers in this house, such as Hon. Clifford Sifton. Between 1895 and 1914 Canada doubled her population with the admission of 5 million immigrants. Among the group was my own father, who came over in 1906. I know there are very difficult problems in connection with immigration, just as there are in
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale regard to other situations. Surely, the government which professes to be responsible for the prosperity in Canada at the present time, and all the other wonderful benefits, could find a solution to this difficulty. I know there are problems of assimilation, problems of housing, social welfare, general employment and economic dislocation as the result of an influx of population. We need people,, however. Other countries have surplus population and we have the room. The only obvious solution is a continued policy of immigration.
Again volunteer community effort is expressing itself in this regard. Here perhaps our biggest job is assimilation. We have the Canadian citizenship council in the field, as well as the various groups from the Canadian Legion, the Y.M.C.A. and various church groups who are trying to deal, on a local level, with this problem of assimilating our new Canadian citizens. I am sure that had our community life, the feeling of neighbourliness, not tended to disintegrate as a result of the neglect of municipalities and so forth, there would have been an even keener participation on the local level in this very important problem of immigration.
It of course remains to be said that, notwithstanding the industrialization and the problem of population arising therefrom, agriculture is still the basic industry of the prairies. Our agricultural industry is perhaps not as unstable as it was formerly, but it still suffers from relative instability from time to time. We hear protests from the producers. Before I make some general observations in this regard I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) concerning the P.F.A.A. I have run into some difficulties in connection with farmers who have suffered crop loss from hail damage. There is no possibility of assistance because of the present large areas required under the act. Hail damage is a special problem.
At the present time farm costs are going up and income is going down. I think it is fair to conclude that only a succession of bumper crops has kept the agricultural economy of the prairies afloat. As is well known to the members of the house, the present crop is the largest we have ever gathered on the prairies. The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) made a reference the other night to the drop in the price index and gave credit, as is usually the case in observations from that side of the house, to the government. Actually the decline in the price index is at the expense of our prairie producers. Returns from produce are going down and costs are going up.
166	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Hinsdale The farmer is even suffering from the high value of the Canadian dollar, because being a producer he is being sacrificed for the American investor.
The lyrical tributes we find in various United States periodicals of recent date are indicative that our friends across the border take a favourable view of the present exchange rate between the Canadian dollar and the United States dollar. It is estimated that out of our bumper crop the farmer will actually receive a half million dollars less than he would have received had the dollar been at par. I am not going to deal with that problem, other than to say that it seems that all down the line the people in the continental west, the prairie people, seem to get into difficulty as compared with the more favourably situated people in central Canada. I say that, regardless of the transition taking place, we still must take an interest in our agricultural economy, and it is not without some reason that the various agricultural organizations on the prairies, particularly the farmers' unions, are now advocating that general discussions be held on agricultural policies.
To sum up my remarks, the difficulties I have outlined with respect to inequitable development across the prairies, concentration in the central provinces, high taxation, extravagance and so forth are inevitable under the present parliamentary situation in Canada. We have lived through three very unhealthy years politically with an overwhelming government majority in the house. We find that by appeals to a broad crosssection of the people on the basis of what you might call phony liberalism, by appeals to state welfarism and expounding the idea that the state can solve all problems, we have developed a situation of political imbalance in Canada. There have been more cautious statements recently, and I was quite impressed with the remarks the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made when he was out west and told the people that you do not get anything for nothing. Seemingly it was a belated return to a more basic liberal viewpoint. However, we still have cries that Canada is enjoying an unprecedented period -*f prosperity which is all due to government beneficence or, as it was put in the chamber yesterday quoting a popular song, "You never had it so good."

speechtext: That was what they said in the United States before their election.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Prosperity is not the only thing in a country. Our prosperity is not unending and we must remember that what we have is almost unique to the North American continent. We actually have an


island of prosperity in a sea of poverty, and our responsibilities are all the greater because of that situation. We must also remember that often nations that have entered into a decline have done so at the peak period of prosperity or, as the poet says:
111 fares the land, to hastening ills a prey. Where wealth accumulates, and men decay.
Therefore prosperity is actually no criterion of the actual state of well-being of a country. We admit there is prosperity. We do not deny the fact. But let me read a quotation from what was said recently by Senator Harry F. Byrd, speaking in the United States. He made what I regard as a very penetrating statement on the problem of centralization in the direction of the superstate, the all-powerful state. He said:
Centralized power and purse breed a sinister political philosophy which scorns frugality, efficiency and integrity; which attaches no importance to waste, debt or immorality; which advocates indefinitely the political formula of tax, spend and elect; and which has no scruples against using public money to influence political decisions.
That is inevitable as long as human nature is what it is and regardless of the political complexion of the party that happens to find itself in office over a long period of time. I came across a quotation in the Rivers Gazette, one of our weekly papers in western Manitoba. It is a parody of the 23rd psalm and reads as follows:
The government is my shepherd, I need not work. It allows me to lie down on good jobs; it leadeth me beside still factories.
It destroyeth my initiative; it leads me into paths of the parasite for politics' sake.
Yea. though I walk through the valley of laziness and deficit spending I will fear no evil; for the government is with me; its doles and its vote-getters. they comfort me.
It prepareth an economic Utopia for me by appropriating the earnings of my grandchildren. It filleth my head with baloney; my efficiency runneth over.
Surely the government shall care for me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in a fool's paradise forever.
I thought this was very appropriate in view of certain developments we have seen south of the border and in this country. Actually it is impossible for a group whose vision is obscured by power to see the difficulties and to accept criticisms of extravagance, unnecessary expenditures and so on. A group long in office is pushed by pressure from all its friends, from the spoil seekers, bandwagon climbers and general camp followers. In the final analysis it is only the sovereign voice of the people that can call a halt. It would seem that the day of deliverance is not too far away.
I should like to refer to another matter outside the main points of my remarks. On the orders of the day today I raised a question

with respect to accepting the offer of the volunteer organizations to carry on welfare activities among our armed forces. In replying the minister indicated that there was no change in policy in that regard. Obviously there is considerable interest throughout the country with respect to the problem, and well there might be because we have achieved a level of recruitment in our armed forces that closely parallels a wartime situation. Church groups have been disturbed about the fact that volunteer welfare organizations have been excluded from participation in the welfare activities among the troops which they carried on so effectively and efficiently during world war II. They established an outstanding reputation with respect to their services.
I was most disturbed to discover from the minister's remarks that there is a principle involved of no change in the present policy and that the former type of welfare service is not going to be operated among our Canadian forces. Because of the reputation established by these organizations during the war, I think the only groups that can adequately serve the troops both abroad and in the numerous depots and military establishments at home are those qualified by experience and actual training. The problem confronting welfare organizations among the armed forces is not necessarily a matter of cigarettes, movies and radio programs, the tangible outward things. It is the intangibles that have to be dealt with among military men who find themselves in a difficult social situation, removed from their families, removed from their churches and removed from general community responsibility.
I strongly suggest that if at all possible something should be done to accept the generous offer of these voluntary organizations. It does not necessarily mean having someone from each organization. They could perhaps pool their resources, but surely from their experience in world war II they have accumulated knowledge that can prove invaluable and thus help to deal with the problem of morale which is so important if we are going to produce strong fighting forces in each of the three armed services.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks at this stage of the debate will be very brief. They have been prompted by a charge which a member of the opposition made in the debate yesterday against the administration of the national employment service for which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) is responsible to parliament. Before proceeding farther, however, Mr. Speaker, I find it a very pleasant duty to join with all speakers who have preceded me in warmly congratulating the mover (Mr. The Address-Mr. P. E. Cote Deslieres) and seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have set for themselves a high standard of discussion which will inspire them both in their further participation in debates in this chamber. I offer them my sincerest wishes for success.
In his speech yesterday the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) resorted, in my view, to tactics which I like to believe will appear outside this house as a hopeless attempt to catch the eye of the public and further the advancement of his party's interests; because it was done without too much concern for the principles of truth and righteousness.
The official opposition has been anxiously searching in the past few months in the administration of various departments for material which they could use to support their irresponsible charges of waste and extravagance by the government. The most they could achieve in their search was to get and put together bits and pieces of information which could give a semblance of truth to their charges against the government, but which in no instance stand the test of conscientious and objective analysis.
The part of the speech by the hon. member for Eglinton which had to do with the Department of Labour received generous hospitality in the columns of the Globe and Mail this morning, but no other paper I know of has carried any reference to it. I would assume that the latter were all convinced of the emptiness of that particular attack of my hon. friend; and if that is their judgment I fully concur.
Since the last war ended our national employment service has made great strides toward improving its machinery and technique for increasing the production of the country by maintaining our labour force at work where it can best serve, and by reducing to the bare minimum the unavoidable periods of unemployment which are characteristic of certain trades and industry in Canada. I could have much to say on that subject but I will leave it for another opportunity in this debate or later in the session.
For the moment I would like to call attention to the Montreal office, which was the office criticized by the hon. member for Eglinton yesterday. The Montreal branch of the national employment service, as is the case with any other branch, is assisted in its work by a local employment committee formed by representatives of industry, labour and the main organizations in the community, both social and business. It is an advisory committee. Their advice has contributed in

The Address-Mr. P. E. Cote the past to the launching of a campaign of publicity and education to develop the trust and eventual co-operation of all parties in industry with the facilities offered by the national employment service. These endeavours have been carried out by means of film showings, newspaper releases, articles, radio talks and personal contacts with employers.
At the Montreal office level, meetings with the advisory committee and other contacts with employers have been followed up during the past five years by the publication of a monthly bulletin. This bulletin is not a publication designed for the public at large. It has a circulation limited to 1,200, 1,000 copies going to the most influential employers of the metropolitan area and about 200 to trade unions, social and business organizations. Often when the bulletin deals with one category of job applicants only, for instance sales and clerical, professional and executive or handicapped and older workers, the bulletin may be sent out to only from 300 to 500, only to those among employers who may have a definite interest in the eventual hiring of that class of applicant. The cost of this bulletin at its very top circulation may run between $20 and $25 a month exclusive of postage. It is in mimeographed form and usually contains from three to five pages. The editor of this monthly bulletin puts together all the resources of his knowledge and ingenuity to make the publication one which will appeal to the employer and be spared from the wastepaper basket for some time at least after it is received.
Usually the bulletin opens with a thought on the plight of the unemployed and the imperative duty for an employer in a country like ours to humanize his handling of employees. The next two or three pages carry a list of job applicants. Their names are omitted purposely and they are referred to by index numbers, by their age and special qualifications. This bulletin issued by the Montreal employment service office has done a great job in the past five years and can still render valuable service. The hon. member for Eglinton may disagree with its editor and the quality of his literature, on the propriety of its quotations or the thoughts which the editor aims to impress upon the minds of employers; but my hon. friend will appreciate from the figures I will give him in a moment that the bulletin in its present form has effectively served its purpose as a liaison agent between the employers and the employment service and as an active factor of effective co-operation between the two.
The total number of placements by the national employment service of Canada for the calendar year 1951 was 926,149. Of that 

total Montreal contributed 113,705 or 12 per cent. In the section of handicapped and older workers falling in that category, for the year 1951 the total placements for Canada have been 14,344, of which Montreal contributed 4,097 or 28-5 per cent. For this year, up to October 30, the proportion is still higher at 29-5 per cent, Montreal having contributed 3,696 placements of applicants in a total for all of Canada of 12,516 handicapped or older workers.
It was with those figures in mind that I interjected during my hon. friend's speech yesterday that Montreal had about the best record in the whole of Canada for the placement of handicapped and older workers. I should now like to get back to what the hon. member had to say of that bulletin which has been an important factor in the successful placement of unemployed in Montreal. Yesterday afternoon, brandishing the last issue of the bulletin in his hand, the hon. member exclaimed, as reported at page 115 of Hansard:
... I hold the government responsible for the profligate waste of the taxpayers' money on rubbish such as this.
The poetry as to which my hon. friend has offered his comment is not new. I am sure it is known to many of the members of this house. In line with the course of action outlined to him by the local employment committee, the editor of the bulletin had chosen that poetry to combat a modern economic tendency by conveying to the mind of management that it is often inhuman to lay off the worker who has reached the age when it will be most difficult for him to find another job. It was intended to be a caution call, a stop and think twice advice to employers who may be about to dispense with the services of an ageing or disabled worker. To be effective, you have to talk to management as well as to labour in a language which will impress them and which they will understand. If the hon. member for Eglinton would now look at this bulletin again and read that poetry, as to which he tried to make so much yesterday, and do it in the light of the information and the circumstances which I have just recited, I am sure he will have altogether different language to use in his comments on it. Fair-minded as I know him to be, he would have only words of praise for the Montreal office and its advisory committee who sponsor this bulletin which costs so little to the public- a mere $20 a month-and which has been so important a factor in the gaining of such an enviable record for the Montreal office in the placement of older workers, handicapped workers and the unemployed generally.

Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to say just a word of comment on certain criticism which the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) made last Tuesday. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) has already replied to one of his attacks. I do not intend to come back to that particular part of his speech. Turning to Hansard, at page 84 I notice that the hon. member, at the opening of his remarks, tried to make an eloquent appeal which is recorded as follows:
I want to deal with a great injustice which exists under the Unemployment Insurance Act and which I believe is long overdue for correction. I am referring to the refusal of the government to pay unemployment insurance which a man or woman has standing to his or her credit when that person becomes incapacitated and is unable to continue to work.
I wish to say to my hon. friend that this matter has been discussed quite often since the act came into operation on July 1, 1941, but the administration have always held to the same course, which is that as long as this act is one to deal with unemployment insurance, there is no possibility that its coverage may be extended beyond the scope which was determined in the act by parliament. This is an act of parliament which has been amended quite often in the past ten or eleven years. This fact will indicate the desire and the readiness of the Minister of Labour and of the administration to improve this act more and more in accordance with suggestions which come from organized labour, management and other responsible organizations in this country.
We are still willing-and I think I can speak for the Minister of Labour in saying this-to try to improve upon what we have achieved in the coverage of this act. We shall do it with the guidance of the unemployment insurance advisory committee which is composed of representatives of organized labour, of industry, and of Canada generally. As we go on I think the country, and labour more particularly, will realize that in this government, and more particularly in the Department of Labour, they have real friends who are anxious to provide social assistance to any extent that this parliament will allow.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first to congratulate-not because it is the custom but because they deserve it- the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both have discharged their duties in a remarkable way, a fact which justifies the confidence reposed 68108-12
The Address-Mr. Dupuis in them by the government. I also extend my compliments to the two newly-appointed ministers, namely the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Campney). The vast experience which they acquired as parliamentary assistants to ministers of the crown and their wide knowledge of public affairs gives assurance that they will perform their functions to the benefit of their respective departments as well as to the advantage of the community.
By reading carefully the speech from the throne one will notice that it contains suggestions which are proper to the present government; that is, the putting into practice of sound policies, such as those applied in the past, in all spheres of our national activity. *In other words it is a program of future realizations to be added to all the good measures put forward and realized by the present Liberal administration for the good of the people.
The leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew) has the thankless task of expressing the point of view of his party. He has measured up to expectations. On the other hand the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in his magnificent address, among many other interesting matters with which he dealt, said, as recorded at page 34 of Hansard:
It is a part of our democratic institutions that there should be someone recognized in our official organizations whose duty it is to watch and criticize what is being done by the advisers of the crown, and I think it is helpful that that should be so. For three and a half years now the government has been attempting to discharge the mandate entrusted to it in 1949. It has not had too much time available to answer criticism, but it has always given close attention to criticism and has always been as attentive as it could be to remedy such weaknesses as the criticism revealed.
These words show the real picture of our Prime Minister, and are a reflection of his good faith and intentions. Never has he turned a deaf ear to what he considered to be good suggestions, regardless of the side of the house from which they came. That is what I call real statesmanship.
Let us see how far the government went in the realization of the program submitted for the approval of the electorate in 1949. The Liberal party at that time, as it always had, stood for the social welfare and the unity of all Canadians. In accordance with their declarations the Liberals, once in office, have made it their duty to adopt measures in order to improve the conditions of life of the less fortunate without neglecting the interests of the others. I mention as examples measures such as that extending old age pensions to the category of people of 65 years of age to 70, and also that providing

The Address-Mr. Dupuis for the universal pension to those above that age. They have also increased the veterans' pensions and established pensions for the blind. They have also awarded an increase in wages to the civil servants. The grants to hospitals and contributions to health laboratories or clinics in every province amount to millions of dollars, which indicates the solicitude of the government towards tne improvement of health conditions and adequate treatment in Canada.
This brings me, incidentally, to a part of the amendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell), concerning a health insurance program, which reads as follows:
We regret further that Your Excellency's advisers have failed:
(a) To recommend legislation establishing a nation-wide health insurance program, with provision for provincial administration.
I know that such a program exists in the province of Saskatchewan, and has existed for a few years. It seems to have given satisfactory results. I know that special attention is being given at the present time, and has been for some time past, to the establishment of a similar plan on a national basis; but I am of the opinion of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), whose words were interpreted as follows by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), as reported in Hansard of November 26 at page 102:
What the hon. member for Peace River asserted was that we are in favour of a national health insurance scheme, to commence at the earliest possible time; but he cautioned the house against any overeager effort on the part of anyone to catapult this nation or the state into any comprehensive scheme of health insurance or hospitalization before the means are available or the facilities are ready for it. The Social Credit leader indicated that the kind of health insurance scheme which we envision would first ensure that we have sufficient doctors, dentists, technicians, clinics and hospital beds available in order to provide the services for all our people under a national health insurance scheme.
This point of view, which I fully endorse, is real wisdom. I know this government is giving this important matter its constant attention, and I am quite sure that in due time, after surveys have been made and necessary precautions taken, and availability of adequate hospitalization assured, a national health insurance program will be added to the many realizations of the party actually in power.
Now let us come back to what this government has done during its present term of office. Many things were said by the opposition in the discussion on the amendment to the Combines Investigation Act, introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), dealing with fixed retail prices. This measure has
IMr. Dupuis.]
given good results, except with regard to a few low-cost articles and in particular cigarettes, on which the profit is so low. The abolition of fixed prices on medium or high-priced articles has helped in lowering the cost of living.
In addition to many other opportune measures assuring social security, housing has been given special care and labour problems also have found salutary solutions. The St. Lawrence seaway project is under way; so is the trans-Canada highway, and vast projects of public works are under study.
What has been the most important problem for the government is to assure adequate national defence in order (a) to provide the forces to defend Canada against attack; (b) to provide operational and administrative staffs, equipment, training personnel and secure organization capable of rapid expansion; (c) to work out with other free nations plans for joint defence based on self-help and mutual aid as part of a combined effort to preserve peace and to restrain aggression.
I remember in the early days of my coming to parliament speeches from members of the opposition in which they reproached the government for its lack of real leadership in the face of the sad outlook caused by the opening of hostilities in Korea. These members stated in a combined movement of unsound criticism that Canada was not ready to face the situation. Time has shown that this pessimism was manifested only to serve political purposes. The participation of Canada in the united action of all free nations has been beyond all expectations. Although nothing must be spared, our country is ready to face any aggression. We paid the price for such protection and, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said, it is the premium paid for the assurance of the survival of democracy.
All these expenses for national defence obviously cannot be made without carrying with them a heavy burden of taxation. Let the menace of war disappear and taxes will accordingly decrease in proportion. Everyone in this house knows that nearly half of all our revenues serves to assure adequate national defence. How can we slow down our efforts in that direction without endangering the lives of our nation and of our allies. Thank God there seems to be place for hope that the danger of war is less and less imminent. Nevertheless no one would suggest, I am sure, that we should cease immediately to prepare ourselves for the eventuality of an unexpected aggression. Hence we must not foresee for some time the complete disappearance of the taxes imposed for national defence purposes, although we might expect a diminution, owing to the fact

previously mentioned, namely the absence of immediate danger of war. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the one who will be the most happy to reduce taxes is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). First of all, as a citizen, he has to contribute himself; and second, knowing his natural disposition, I can assert that he will not fail to seize the first opportunity to alleviate the burden imposed on the shoulders of the taxpayers. As all observe, we foresee an increase of production and business and undoubtedly, if prospects are such as they seem to be for the coming year, he will certainly take into account this eventual situation when preparing the next budget.
I am pleased to see him a little more optimistic. Let us hope that this optimism presages good news for Canadians in the taxation field. Although sometimes his decisions were not a source of popularity for the Minister of Finance, he has never shifted his responsibilities. He has been the advocate of the pay-as-you-go policy, avoiding a heavy mortgage on future generations.
Since I am talking of the budget for the coming fiscal year, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the necessity of changing the rate of income tax especially for married people and the heads of families. I know that a couple of years ago-not on the eve of an election, mind you-the scale of deduction was increased, but I respectfully submit that there is place for improvement in this connection. Again I also suggest that all revenues derived from stock market profits, or sales of businesses, should be taxed at the source when the transaction takes place. I know of some people selling their stores and properties and realizing a profit of thousands of dollars after only a few years of possession. Fortunes have been realized in stock market transactions without any sort of tax being imposed on the beneficiaries.
I ardently hope that the rate of excise tax imposed on cigarettes will be again decreased, and for many reasons, the principal one being the urgent need of putting an end to smuggling, which has become the greatest competitor of the manufacturers of this product. These manufacturers in certain cases have been forced to lay off some of their personnel. If the expenditures for defence production are to be less and the rhythm of business increased, these suggestions can be put into effect without fear of a deficit.
There is one particular point I wish to bring to the attention of the government, and that is the necessity of studying the opportunity of imposing higher duties on raw materials being exported, if it is at all possible to do so. I shall mention one only, although a 68108-124
The Address-Mr. Dupuis complete revision should be made in respect of other products. I would make particular mention of raw furs, which are bought here at a low price, used on a wide scale in the manufacture of coats and all sorts of other garments, and which are dumped here afterwards at very low prices, due to mass production which is carried out particularly in the United States. The result is that our fur workers are kept idle many months of the year when they could be employed manufacturing these products, if it were not for the unfair competition they cannot meet.
Coming back to the reduction of taxes, one must bear in mind the fact that this would not be possible if the government were to listen to the suggestions coming from the opposite side of the house from hon. members who illogically call for increased expenditures approaching some $600 million and demand at the same time a diminution in taxes.

increased expenditures; that is far from the fact.

speechtext: No; I heard your leader, and the hon. member for Eglinton at the same time, proposing all sorts of expenditures while at the same time asking diminution in taxation. I heard that.

speechtext: No, you did not hear that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, if you did not say it I am afraid you are going to be reproached by your chief. Enough has been said on this subject, so that I shall not take more time in offering proof as to how inconsistent these suggestions are. It is evident that this kind of opposition is only an attempt to get votes at the next election. Well, let me tell my hon. friends that they are wasting their time, because the people of this country have enough sense to read the minds of these alleged saviours, and to realize their lack of sincerity and seriousness.
An appeal to the people is expected during the course of the next year. Already all sorts of prognostications are in the air. These are not very promising for any of the opposition

The Address-Mr. Dupuis parties, and if there is any doubt in their minds I would refer their supporters to the Gallup poll inquiries which indicate, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Bona-venture (Mr. Arsenault), that the stock of the Conservative party has dropped even faster than has the cost of living index in this country. The same will be the fate of the other two parties, if the predictions of the article which appears in the Evening Citizen of November 20 are realized. This article was quoted by the hon. member to whom I have just referred, and reads as follows:
There is not just one opposition party, as in the United States, striving to push the government out of power, but three, and no one of them has shown any sign of rising to a really dominant position over the others. The Liberals, on the other hand, have in Mr. St. Laurent a leader whose prestige stands high throughout the country. Especially is this true of his own province, and no Canadian political party can hope to win office without showing marked strength in Quebec.
I understand the opponents of the Liberal party will use the slogan which some people believe contributed in a high degree to the victory of General Eisenhower in the recent American election. That was the slogan "It's time for a change".

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, you will not say "Hear, hear" in a while. Just listen to the rest of what I have to say. It's time for a change- not on this side of the house, but on your side-a change in the ideals you have set out in the past, a change in the principles of your party.
What a disillusionment! Everyone knows that the situation created by the Democratic party in the United States through scandals connected with high-ranking Democratic public servants does not apply in Canada, or to this Liberal government. This is the government which held office throughout the last war, handling and spending billions of dollars, and without a single scandal.

speechtext: Is that how you beat the Liberal in St. Mary?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I did not beat any Liberal in St. Mary. I was a Liberal myself, and I thought I would be a better representative than my opponent. Some other people thought the same way, and I am here.
In Canada we can depend on the honesty of our public servants, and that of this Liberal government which, during its long term of office, has never been suspected of corruption of any sort. Eisenhower has to his credit a life entirely devoted and heroically consecrated to his country. I wonder if we could find a person with such merit in the ranks of the opposition, so they might feel that they have a chance to take office after the next appeal to the people.
Other factors, such as controversies in connection with the settlement of labour questions, and the part taken by the United States in international affairs, have engaged the attention of our neighbours, and there is no doubt that these factors influenced the verdict of the electors in that country. In Canada the achievement of the Liberal party in all spheres of our national economy is the assurance of the confidence it will receive from the Canadian people. Under the direction of its most worthy chief, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, the Liberal party can face the coming appeal to the people with serenity.
